citeAs: Masry, A., Long, D. X., Tan, J. Q., Joty, S., & Hoque, E. (2022). ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. ACL 2022 Findings.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque (York University, Nanyang Technological University, Salesforce Research)
description: ChartQA is a large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts, covering 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 machine-generated questions from human-written chart summaries. The benchmark consists of 20,882 charts curated from four different online sources (Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, OECD) and focuses on complex visual and logical reasoning questions involving arithmetic and logical operations.
name: ChartQA
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each chart received 2 questions from one worker; each question was then answered by a second annotator for verification.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk crowdworkers with acceptance rate ≥95% and ≥5000 accomplished HITs, further filtered via a pre-test. Annotators were compensated at the US minimum wage rate ($7.25/hour), receiving $0.60 per task (estimated 3-5 minutes per task). All annotations were anonymized.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-annotator agreement based on exact matches was 61.04%. A manual check on 500 random samples found agreement of 78.55% when considering typos and lexical variations (e.g., "3$" vs "3 dollars"). For machine-generated questions, 86.64% of 1,250 manually analyzed QA pairs were found to be complete, answerable, and correct.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Workers were asked to provide two types of questions per chart: compositional questions (involving at least two mathematical/logical operations) and visual questions (referring to visual attributes of marks). In each HIT, workers verified two previously asked questions and provided two new QA pairs. Workers with acceptance rate ≥95% and ≥5000 accomplished HITs were selected, and further filtered via a pre-test. The same questions were answered by a second annotator; if both answers matched exactly, the answer was accepted; otherwise, answers were manually checked.
rai:dataBiases: Politics is a common topic among all sources, particularly in the Pew dataset where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type (79.4% simple, 20.6% complex). The dataset was curated from four different sources to ensure variety in visual styles and topics.
rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from four online sources: Statista (statista.com), Pew Research (pewresearch.org), Our World In Data (ourworldindata.org), and OECD (oecd.org). For Pew, only chart images were crawled. For the other three, underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and associated text descriptions were also extracted.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Chart images, underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG files, and associated text descriptions crawled from Statista, Pew Research, OWID, and OECD. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files.
rai:dataLimitations: Models perform worse when the gold data table is not provided, highlighting challenges in automatic data extraction from real-world charts with diverse styles. Current approaches for automatic data extraction are modular and error-prone. The dataset only covers bar, line, and pie chart types.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Dataset augmentation was performed by fine-tuning a T5 model on SQuAD and applying it to human-written Statista chart summaries to automatically generate 23,111 additional questions. The process involved two T5 models: one for answer extraction and one for answer-aware question generation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For machine-generated questions, a heuristic filter was applied to remove invalid questions where the answer cannot be found in the chart data table. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions. Both human-written and machine-generated QA pairs were randomly split into train, validation, and test sets.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The models trained on this dataset can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. The dataset was collected respecting intellectual property rights and terms of use of the source platforms.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmark for evaluating chart question answering systems that involve visual and logical reasoning. Intended to help develop and evaluate models that can answer complex reasoning questions about real-world charts, including compositional and visual questions.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model (fine-tuned on SQuAD) used for answer extraction and question generation from human-written chart summaries; ChartOCR model (Luo et al., 2021) used for automatic chart data extraction; CRAFT model (Baek et al., 2019) used for text recognition in chart elements.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotator identities were anonymized. No personal information about chart subjects is collected; charts cover public topics such as economy, politics, health, and society.

null_reasons.license: No single dataset license is stated; the paper describes per-source terms of use (Statista for academic use, Pew with attribution, OECD open, OWID open access) but no unified license for the dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe or date range for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No explicit discussion of missing data handling in the collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan described in the paper.

evidence.name: In this work, we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9.6K human-written questions as well as 23.1K questions generated from human-written chart summaries.
evidence.description: we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9,608 human-written questions focusing on logical and visual reasoning questions. Since human annotations are costly, we also generated another 23,111 questions automatically from human-written chart summaries using a T5 model. Our benchmark consists of 20,882 charts which are curated from four different online sources to ensure variety in visual styles and topics.

evidence.rai:dataCollection: we crawled charts from four different sources: (i) Statista (statista.com) is an online platform that presents charts covering a variety of topics including economy, politics, and industry. (ii) The Pew research (pewresearch.org) publishes report about social and economic issues, demographic trends and public opinion with a wide variety of charts. (iii) Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org) is another platform that contains thousands of charts about different global issues such as economy, finance, and society. (iv) Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development or OECD (oecd.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: we crawled charts from four different sources: (i) Statista (statista.com) is an online platform that presents charts covering a variety of topics including economy, politics, and industry.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: For the other three, we extracted the underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG ﬁle and associate text description. Finally, we extracted the bounding boxes information of the different chart elements (e.g., x-axis labels) from the SVG ﬁles to train our data extraction models.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: We have two main annotations procedures: (i) collect human-authored QA pairs using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) and (ii) generate QA pairs from the Statista human-written summaries.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: In each HIT (Human Intelligent Task), the workers verify two previously asked questions by other workers and also provide two new QA pairs. To ensure quality, we selected workers with an acceptance rate of 95% and total accomplished HITs of 5000. Moreover, we further ﬁltered the workers by giving them a pre-test to select the best qualiﬁed workers for this task.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: For each chart, the workers provide two questions with the answers. The same questions are then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly match, we consider the answer to be correct.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Overall, the agreement between the crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. However, such exact match does not consider typos or lexical variations (e.g., 3$ vs. 3 dollars, 86.33 vs 86.3) that are common in human annotation. Hence, we have also manually checked the agreement on 500 random samples and found the agreement to be much higher (78.55%) when we consider typos and lexical variations.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: In order to fairly compensate the Mechanical Turk annotators, we considered the minimum wage in the United States at the time ($7.25 USD per hour). The estimated time taken for each task is 3-5 minutes. Hence, these annotators received $0.6 USD for each task. Additionally, to protect the privacy of these annotators, all of their annotations were anonymized.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: To ﬁlter out such invalid questions, we developed a simple heuristic where we ﬁlter out the question if the answer cannot be found in the chart data table. Moreover, for the sake of fair evaluation, we manually cleaned the test set of the machine generated dataset by removing invalid questions.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: we ﬁne-tune a pre-trained T5 model on the SQuAD QA dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) and apply to the human-written chart summaries that come with the charts from Statista to automatically generate questions that are human-like with sufﬁcient lexical and syntactic variations. The process involves training and applying two T5 models: one for answer extraction and the other for answer-aware question generation.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: we ﬁne-tune a pre-trained T5 model on the SQuAD QA dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) and apply to the human-written chart summaries that come with the charts from Statista to automatically generate questions that are human-like with sufﬁcient lexical and syntactic variations.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We present ChartQA, a new large-scale benchmark with human-written questions focusing on visual and logical reasoning. We hope that our benchmark will serve as a starting point for others to address these challenges.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Our models can be abused to mislead the public about the charts content and implications. While our models provide state-of-the-art results on most of the existing datasets, we can not guarantee that their output will be correct all the time.
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Additionally, to protect the privacy of these annotators, all of their annotations were anonymized.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Table 5 indicates that performance of our models decrease when the gold table is not given, suggesting the need for more accurate data extraction. Current approaches for automatic data extraction are modular and combine deep learning and rule-based methods which are error-prone.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Politics is a common topic among all sources but particularly in the Pew dataset where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4 %). Other common topics include economy, health, and society.
